title: Gradient descent and backpropagation on computational graphs
summary: The gradient as the steepest-ascent direction; gradient descent and its exact analysis on quadratics (step-size threshold, condition number, best rate); the descent lemma for smooth functions; computational graphs; backpropagation as the chain rule in reverse topological order and its cost; autograd and the training loop.

objectives.description: Prove that the negative gradient is the steepest-descent direction and analyse gradient descent on a quadratic: convergence iff 0 < η < 2/λ_max, contraction factor, condition number and best rate (κ−1)/(κ+1).
State and prove the descent lemma for β-smooth functions and deduce that gradient descent with η ≤ 1/β reaches points of arbitrarily small gradient.
Compute every parameter gradient of a small network by the reverse-mode chain rule on its computational graph, verify one by finite differences, and explain the cost of reverse versus forward mode.
Write a correct training loop with autograd, including zeroing accumulated gradients, and explain what each line does.

preparation.description: Read W1D2 Tutorial 1, Section 1.1 (Gradients & Steepest Ascent) and attempt its Analytical Exercise 1.1 before reading the lesson's proof.
Read Section 1.2 (Gradient Descent Algorithm) and Section 1.3 (Computational Graphs and Backprop), including the optional chain-rule exercise.
Read Section 2.2 (Backward Propagation) and Section 3.1 (Training loop in PyTorch); note where gradients are zeroed.

activities.title: Lesson with W1D2 Tutorial 1
activities.instructions: Read the lesson alongside the tutorial. After the quadratic example, close everything and re-derive the condition 0 < η < 2/λ_max on paper before reading on. Check the hand-backprop example line by line.

activities.title: Lab: the gradient-descent surface
activities.instructions: Prediction first: write down the learning rate at which you expect divergence on the quadratic with eigenvalues 1 and 10, and the rate you expect to be fastest. Then run η = 0.05, 0.1, 0.18 and 0.21, record what happens along each eigendirection, and compare with your predictions. Finish on the non-convex surface by finding a start that ends at a stationary point that is not the minimum.

activities.title: Tutorial: backprop by hand; step sizes on a quadratic
activities.instructions: Attempt exercise 1 before asking for any hint, and verify one gradient numerically. Then exercise 2. Submit each attempt when you believe it is complete; revise after feedback.

activities.title: Explain: why reverse mode
activities.instructions: Write exercise 3 without the lesson open, then compare with the lesson's Model (reverse-mode differentiation).

activities.title: Retrieval: the unit's statements
activities.instructions: From memory: the steepest-ascent proposition; the convergence condition and best rate for a quadratic; the descent lemma; the adjoint recursion; the five lines of a training loop.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: all eight adjoints computed by the reverse sweep, the gradient step applied correctly, and one derivative confirmed by finite differences.

commonMisconceptions.claim: A smaller learning rate is always safer, so start small and leave it.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Below 2/λ_max every step converges; the question is speed. On a quadratic the best step is 2/(λ_min + λ_max), and halving it roughly doubles the number of steps. Safety has a precise threshold; below it, smaller is slower, not safer.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Backpropagation is a separate algorithm from the chain rule, or needs the loss to be differentiable everywhere.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It is the multivariable chain rule evaluated in reverse topological order on the computational graph. At kinks autograd returns a chosen subgradient; the derivative does not exist there, and the method still works in practice.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Calling backward() computes the gradient and replaces the previous one.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Gradients accumulate into .grad by design. Without zero_grad the previous step's gradient is added to the current one and the algorithm being run is no longer gradient descent.
